chapter_title: Sending Transactions to Smart Contract Functions (State-Changing)

screens.title: Send State-Changing Transactions with send()
screens.subtitle: How Web3.js constructs, signs, broadcasts, and confirms state changes on Ethereum

narration.text: In this lesson we'll learn how Web3. js performs state-changing operations using the send method. You will see how a call that modifies contract state becomes a signed transaction, how gas determines whether it will run, and how the network confirms the change. We'll ground these ideas with two practical examples: storing a value in a Storage contract and incrementing a Counter. Knowing these steps is essential because any change to blockchain state consumes gas and requires a signed sender account. That means the frontend, a wallet like MetaMask, or server-side code must prepare and sign the transaction correctly. We'll also cover how to estimate gas with web3. eth. estimateGas, how to read the transaction receipt to confirm success and events, and common errors you will encounter, like out-of-gas, revert, and insufficient funds. By the end you'll be able to send a transaction, handle the receipt, and give clear feedback to users about pending and confirmed transactions — skills crucial for any interactive dApp.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: send() turns a state-changing call into a signed, gas-paid transaction that is broadcast and mined; the receipt confirms success and provides gas and event details.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after completing this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives guide the practical skills you will gain. First, you will be able to execute state-changing functions using contract. methods. myFunction(). send by preparing the necessary options and sender account. That matters because send is the entry point for any operation that writes on-chain. Second, you will understand why a sender account, a private key or wallet, and gas are required. In practice this means knowing where signing happens — in MetaMask for browser flows or with signTransaction in Node — and who pays gas. Third, you will learn the transaction lifecycle: how a transaction is created, signed, broadcast, mined, and confirmed, and how to examine the transaction receipt for transactionHash, gasUsed, and emitted events. Finally, you will learn to estimate gas and handle common errors like out-of-gas, revert, and insufficient funds. Together these objectives let you send reliable transactions and interpret the results, which is essential for building responsive dApps.

screens.title: What send() Does
screens.subtitle: From a method call to a signed, broadcast transaction

narration.text: send() is the Web3. js entry point for state-changing contract calls. When you invoke contract. methods. myStateChangingFunction(). send with options, Web3 constructs a transaction object that includes the contract address as the recipient, encoded function call data, the sender address, gas settings, and any Ether value to send. The process continues by signing the transaction with the sender's private key or via a wallet, then broadcasting that signed transaction to an Ethereum node which relays it to the network. The important distinction from call-based reads is that send() writes to global state and consumes gas. For example, calling a Storage contract's store function with send will change the contract's stored value and may emit events. A common misconception is to treat send like call; remember that send requires signing and gas payment, while call only reads data off-chain without signing. In practice, send() is used whenever a dApp must update contract state, trigger events, or move Ether inside the contract. Always verify the sender address and gas assumptions before sending to avoid failed or costly transactions. What send() Does means send() packages a state-changing function call into a signed transaction that is broadcast to the network and paid for with gas.. In practical terms, from a method call to a signed, broadcast transaction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What send() Does
Definition

send() creates and submits transactions

send() is required for any function that modifies contract state or sends Ether. It prepares a transaction object containing to, data, from, gas, gasPrice, and value, then signs and broadcasts it.

Transaction snapshot
{ to: contractAddress,
  data: encodedCall,
  from: senderAccount,
  gas: gasLimit,
  gasPrice: gasPrice,
  value: weiValue }
Supporting points
  • send() modifies on-chain state and therefore consumes gas measured in units paid in Ether.
  • The transaction must be signed by the sender; in browser flows a wallet handles signing, in Node.js you sign directly.
  • Once mined, a receipt is returned containing transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, and events.
Key takeaway
Use send() when your function changes state; always provide a signed from and sensible gas settings.

screens.title: Transaction Lifecycle
screens.subtitle: Create, sign, broadcast, mine, and confirm

narration.text: A transaction moves through a predictable lifecycle that you must monitor to confirm state changes. First, your dApp or Web3. js call assembles a transaction object with the recipient address, encoded data, optional Ether value, and gas settings. Next, the sender signs the transaction — either via a wallet like MetaMask or by using a private key to produce a signature in Node. js. After signing, the signed transaction is sent to an Ethereum node and enters the network's pending pool. Miners select pending transactions, include them in a block, and when that block is added, the transaction becomes confirmed. At that point Web3. js returns a transaction receipt containing transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, and any events emitted. A practical example is calling Storage. store via send: after the receipt appears, verify the stored value with a separate call. A common misconception is that the appearance of a transaction hash means the state changed — it only means the transaction was broadcast; you must wait for the receipt to be certain. Always present clear pending and confirmation states to users until the receipt arrives.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Monitor a transaction from creation through receipt to confirm the on-chain state change reliably.

content.html:

Process Flow

Create → Sign → Broadcast → Mine → Confirm

1. Create
2. Sign
3. Broadcast
4. Mine
5. Receipt
Creating encodes the function call and sets gas and value. Signing authenticates the sender. Broadcasting delivers the signed transaction to nodes. Mining includes it in a block. The receipt confirms execution and returns gasUsed and events.
Remember: a transaction hash indicates broadcast; only the mined receipt guarantees state change and returned events.
Example

receipt.transactionHash
receipt.blockNumber
receipt.gasUsed
receipt.events

screens.title: Signing: MetaMask vs Node.js
screens.subtitle: Who signs transactions and where private keys live

narration.text: Signing is the step that binds a transaction to a sender. In browser environments, a user wallet like MetaMask handles signing: the dApp sends a transaction request and the wallet prompts the user to confirm and sign using a local, secure key store. This keeps private keys off your servers and gives users control. In contrast, Node. js scripts often sign transactions on the server using web3. eth. accounts. signTransaction with a private key under your control, or by using unlocked local accounts on test nodes like Ganache. Each approach has trade-offs: MetaMask provides user security and consent but requires UI flows and pop-ups; server-side signing offers automation for backend tasks but increases responsibility for key management and security. A key misconception is thinking signing happens implicitly; it always requires the sender's signature. Pick the signing model that fits your trust model and UX: interactive user transactions should use wallets, while backend services or batched operations may require secure server-side signing with robust key protection. Signing: MetaMask vs Node.js means client wallets (metamask) sign in-browser with user consent; node.js can sign programmatically but must protect private keys.. In practical terms, who signs transactions and where private keys live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Signing models

MetaMask (Browser)

Node.js (Server)

  • Useful for automated tasks, but you must secure keys on the server.
  • Test nodes like Ganache may provide unlocked accounts for development.
Tip: Use server signing only with strict key management.
Practical note

Design UI flows so users know when a MetaMask pop-up will appear, and always display the transaction hash and pending status until the receipt confirms the action.

screens.title: Gas: Limit and Price
screens.subtitle: How gas units and price determine transaction cost and success

narration.text: Gas is the unit of computational cost on Ethereum; every EVM operation consumes gas units. When you send a transaction, you must provide a gasLimit — the maximum gas units you are willing to allow — and a gasPrice — how much Ether you will pay per gas unit. The total cost is gasUsed multiplied by gasPrice and is paid by the sender. If a transaction runs longer than the gasLimit, it runs out of gas and reverts, consuming all gas spent up to that point. If gasPrice is too low, miners may delay or ignore the transaction. Newer networks and wallets may use gas fee models beyond a simple gasPrice, but the important practical points remain: estimate the gas requirement accurately and choose a gas price that gets your transaction mined in the desired timeframe. A common mistake is omitting gas options and trusting defaults; use web3. eth. estimateGas for a realistic number and add a small buffer to avoid reverting on complex operations. Always confirm the sender can cover estimatedCost to avoid insufficient funds errors. Gas: Limit and Price means set gaslimit to a safe maximum and gasprice to a value miners will accept; estimate and add a buffer to prevent reverts.. In practical terms, how gas units and price determine transaction cost and success. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas basics

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Gas: Limit and Price
Concept

Gas Limit and Gas Price

Gas limit caps computation. Gas price sets payment per unit. Together they determine cost and whether the transaction completes.

Gas Limit
Maximum gas units you allow. Too low → out-of-gas and revert.
Gas Price
Payment per gas unit. Too low → delayed or ignored by miners.
Practical example
const gasEstimate = await contract.methods.store(42).estimateGas({ from: account });
// Use: gas: gasEstimate + 10000
Add a small buffer to cover minor variance in gas usage. Always check sender's balance can cover gasLimit × gasPrice.

screens.title: Using estimateGas Safely
screens.subtitle: Estimate gas and apply a buffer before sending

narration.text: Estimating gas reduces the chance of an out-of-gas revert. The recommended pattern is to call contract. methods. myFunction(...). estimateGas with a from address to get a realistic prediction, then add a small buffer to account for variable execution paths. For example, when calling Storage. store, call estimateGas and then send with gas: gasEstimate + 10000. The code pattern in Node. js looks like retrieving accounts from web3. eth. getAccounts, calling estimateGas with the same from address, and then using send with the buffered gas limit. One misconception is to rely on a single static gasLimit for all functions; complex contracts may demand varying gas per invocation. Another is to confuse estimateGas with a guarantee — it is a prediction based on the node's simulation and can occasionally be slightly off. So always include a buffer and handle any errors returned by send. This pattern balances cost and safety, preventing many common failures while keeping transactions reasonably priced. Using estimateGas Safely means call estimategas with from, then send with gas set to estimated + safety buffer to avoid reverts.. In practical terms, estimate gas and apply a buffer before sending. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Estimate pattern
keyIdea.text: Call estimateGas with from, then send with gas set to estimated + safety buffer to avoid reverts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Estimate Gas
Pattern
const accounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
const sender = accounts[0];
const gasEstimate = await storageContract.methods.store(42).estimateGas({ from: sender });
const receipt = await storageContract.methods.store(42).send({
  from: sender,
  gas: gasEstimate + 10000
});
console.log('Receipt:', receipt);
Always estimate with the same from address you will use to send. Add a buffer like 10,000 or 10-20% depending on function complexity. Log the estimate for debugging and consider surfacing it to advanced users.
Remember: estimateGas simulates execution and can be slightly lower than final gas used if the state changes between estimation and mining.
Common mistake
Omitting the from field in estimateGas can produce incorrect estimates. Always provide the same sender for accurate results.
Pro tip

Log estimates and actual gasUsed to refine your buffer over time for each contract function.

screens.title: Practical Example: Storage.store() in Node.js
screens.subtitle: Send a transaction, handle the receipt, and verify state

narration.text: Let's walk through the Storage. store example in Node. js. Start by connecting to a provider such as Ganache, create a contract instance with the ABI and deployed address, and get a sender account from web3. eth. getAccounts. Before sending, estimate gas using storageContract. methods. store(value). estimateGas({ from: sender }). With that estimate, call send with a buffered gas limit and await the transaction receipt. The receipt gives you transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, and events emitted during execution; use these fields to confirm the operation. After the receipt is returned, call the contract's read-only retrieve or get function to verify the new state on-chain. A common misconception is that a returned receipt implies successful business logic; instead, inspect events and state to confirm the desired effect. Finally, include try-catch to surface revert reasons or insufficient funds errors and provide user-friendly messages. This sequence — estimate, send, await receipt, verify — is how you reliably change and confirm the blockchain state. Practical Example: Storage.store() in Node.js means estimate gas, send with a buffer, await the receipt, and then verify state with a read call.. In practical terms, send a transaction, handle the receipt, and verify state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Node.js example
keyIdea.text: Estimate gas, send with a buffer, await the receipt, and then verify state with a read call.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Storage.store Node.js
Starter code
import Web3 from 'web3';
import storageAbi from './storageAbi.json';
const provider = new Web3.providers.HttpProvider('http://localhost:8545');
const web3 = new Web3(provider);
const storageContract = new web3.eth.Contract(storageAbi, CONTRACT_ADDRESS);

async function sendStore() {
  const accounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
  const sender = accounts[0];
  const valueToStore = 42;
  const gasEstimate = await storageContract.methods.store(valueToStore).estimateGas({ from: sender });
  const receipt = await storageContract.methods.store(valueToStore).send({ from: sender, gas: gasEstimate + 10000 });
  console.log('Transaction Hash:', receipt.transactionHash);
  console.log('Gas Used:', receipt.gasUsed);
  const updated = await storageContract.methods.retrieve().call();
  console.log('Updated stored data:', parseInt(updated));
}
Explanation
  • estimateGas simulates execution to predict gas usage.
  • send returns a receipt after mining; read it to confirm success.
  • Call retrieve after receipt to verify state change.
Key Takeaway

Always verify the new state after the receipt to ensure your business logic executed as intended.

screens.title: Errors: revert, out of gas, insufficient funds
screens.subtitle: Diagnose and mitigate common transaction failures

narration.text: When sending transactions you will encounter a few common failure modes. A revert happens when a require or revert in the contract logic is triggered; the transaction fails and state changes are rolled back, but gas is still consumed. To diagnose, inspect the error message returned by send — it often contains the revert reason — and check contract preconditions before sending. Out-of-gas occurs if the provided gasLimit is too low for the function's operations. Prevent this by estimating gas and adding a buffer. Insufficient funds arise when the sender does not have enough Ether to cover gasLimit times gasPrice; check balances before submitting. Another practical issue is unlocking accounts for node-managed signing; local test nodes like Ganache often provide unlocked accounts while production nodes require secure signing. To mitigate these errors, validate sender balances, run pre-checks of contract state to avoid predictable reverts, use estimateGas, and show actionable messages in the UI describing the failure and suggested fixes. Errors: revert, out of gas, insufficient funds means detect revert reasons, estimate gas with a buffer, and verify sender balance to prevent and explain transaction failures.. In practical terms, diagnose and mitigate common transaction failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Error handling
keyIdea.text: Detect revert reasons, estimate gas with a buffer, and verify sender balance to prevent and explain transaction failures.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Errors & Diagnosis
Revert
Contract logic prevented execution. State rolled back but gas consumed. Check require conditions and revert reasons in error messages.
Out of gas
Gas limit too low. Use estimateGas and add a buffer to avoid premature termination that still consumes gas.
Insufficient funds
Sender lacks enough Ether to cover gasLimit × gasPrice. Verify balances before sending and present clear error messages.
Mitigation checklist
  • Use estimateGas and add a safety buffer (10-20% or 10,000 units).
  • Pre-check contract state to avoid predictable reverts.
  • Confirm sender balance covers estimated gas cost.
  • Catch errors and show user-friendly guidance: 'increase gas', 'check funds', or 'review inputs'.

screens.title: Increment the Counter — Step-by-step

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Increment Counter Activity
Starter snippet
async function incrementCounter() {
  const accounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
  const sender = accounts[0];
  console.log(`Incrementing from ${sender}`);
  const gasEstimate = await counterContract.methods.increment().estimateGas({ from: sender });
  const receipt = await counterContract.methods.increment().send({ from: sender, gas: gasEstimate + 10000 });
  console.log('Transaction Hash:', receipt.transactionHash);
  console.log('Gas Used:', receipt.gasUsed);
  const newCount = await counterContract.methods.getCount().call();
  console.log('New count:', parseInt(newCount));
}
Checks
  • Ensure Ganache is running and contract deployed.
  • Verify accounts[0] has enough Ether.
  • If out-of-gas, increase the buffer and retry.
Try this

Intentionally set gas: 100 to see an out-of-gas revert, then fix it using estimateGas.

screens.title: User Experience for Pending Transactions
screens.subtitle: How to present pending state, transaction hash, and confirmation

narration.text: A good dApp communicates transaction progress clearly. When a user submits a state-changing action, show an immediate acknowledgement and the transaction hash once available. Explain that the hash means the transaction was broadcast, not yet mined. Provide an explicit pending status and update progress when the receipt arrives. Use the receipt's blockNumber and gasUsed to mark confirmation, and read emitted events to update application state. For long confirmation times, allow users to continue other tasks and display a clear status history listing pending and confirmed transactions. Also include clear error messages with actionable steps: 'increase gas', 'check wallet balance', or 'review inputs'. A common developer mistake is hiding the transaction hash or not updating the UI after the receipt, leaving users unsure whether their action succeeded. By surfacing hashes, receipts, and readable messages, you reduce support friction and improve trust in your dApp. User Experience for Pending Transactions means show the transaction hash immediately, update on receipt, and translate technical errors into clear user actions.. In practical terms, how to present pending state, transaction hash, and confirmation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Production Checklist
screens.subtitle: Gas management, receipts, events, and secure signing

narration.text: Before deploying transaction flows to production, follow a concise checklist. First, always estimate gas and set a buffer tailored to each function. Second, implement robust receipt handling: verify transactionHash, blockNumber, gasUsed, and emitted events, then update state only after the receipt confirms. Third, ensure secure signing: prefer client-side wallets for user interactions and avoid storing private keys on servers when possible. For necessary server-side signing, use secure key storage and rotate keys regularly. Fourth, present clear UX for pending and confirmed transactions and translate low-level errors into actionable messages. Fifth, monitor and log gas usage per function to refine buffers and reduce costs. Finally, design contract logic defensively to minimize revert paths for expected user input. These practices reduce the likelihood of costly failures and improve reliability and trust in your dApp. Production Checklist means estimate gas, handle receipts, secure keys, present clear ux, monitor gas, and design defensive contract logic.. In practical terms, gas management, receipts, events, and secure signing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: To wrap up, focus on three essentials. First, send() converts state-changing calls into signed, broadcast transactions that consume gas; use it whenever your dApp writes to the blockchain. Second, estimate gas and add a buffer; this prevents out-of-gas reverts and gives you a predictable cost structure. Third, always handle receipts and events after a transaction is mined; the receipt confirms execution, shows gas used, and returns emitted events you can use to update your application state. Keep these three concepts central when designing transaction flows, and your dApp will be more reliable and user friendly. Takeaway

These small operational practices reduce failures and improve user confidence.
